idiom_name: none: redefinition instead of overloading; case/when or polymorphic methods at run time
implementation_notes: Ruby does not support overloading and has no static binding: when the def keyword meets an existing method name it simply redefines it (the documentation calls this overriding), so two definitions cannot coexist as alternative implementations of one name. What replaces the classic structure: polymorphic methods on the collaborating objects - the 'replace conditional with polymorphism' refactoring the Ruby community favours - or, for a closed set, a case/when on the object's class or on an explicit type code, both of which are runtime decisions. The classic form is not applicable; even a hand-written tag plus a lookup table is a runtime table, since no selection can happen before the program runs.
code_sketch:
# no overloading: the second definition would replace the first
class Dist
  def self.at(seq, i)
    case seq
    when Array then seq[i]                 # runtime class test (=== on the class)
    else seq.each_with_index { |v, n| return v if n == i }
    end
  end
end

# the Ruby way: put the operation on the type instead
# class Array; def at_seq(i) = self[i]; end
pitfalls: An accidental redefinition silently deletes the other implementation - no error, no warning, last definition wins - so a 'ladder' spread over several files is fragile.

case/when uses Module#=== (so when Numeric matches subclasses, and when Array matches array subclasses), while an explicit is_a? check reads differently and behaves differently for singleton classes; mixing the two gives inconsistent dispatch.
Adding a branch by reopening a class or prepending a module makes the ancestor chain decide which definition wins rather than specificity, so the ladder's order is invisible at the call site.
sources: Ruby documentation (syntax/methods): 'When Ruby encounters the def keyword, it doesn't consider it an error if the method already exists: it simply redefines it. This is called overriding.', https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/syntax/methods_rdoc.html
thoughtbot, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (Ruby Science) - the community's answer to type-based branching, https://thoughtbot.com/ruby-science/replace-conditional-with-polymorphism.html
alternative: Move the operation onto the objects themselves (polymorphism, optionally via modules/prepend) or resolve a closed set with case/when on the class or on a type code. Ruby has no static binding, so the compiler-side selection the pattern relies on cannot exist; a tag can only be inspected at run time.
